notes.definition: Internal energy is the energy stored inside a system by the particles (atoms and molecules) that make it up. It is the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in the system.
explanation: Every material is made of particles that are constantly moving. In a solid they vibrate about fixed positions; in a liquid and a gas they move from place to place. Because they move, the particles have kinetic energy. The particles also exert forces on each other (they attract each other and are held in a particular arrangement), so they have potential energy that depends on their positions relative to each other.

The internal energy of a system is the total of the kinetic energy and the potential energy of all its particles. It is measured in joules (J). Internal energy depends on how many particles there are, so a large amount of a substance at a low temperature, such as a swimming pool, can have more internal energy than a small amount at a high temperature, such as a cup of tea.

Heating a system transfers energy to its particles, which increases the internal energy. This can do one of two things. It can raise the temperature of the system: the particles move faster, so their kinetic energy increases. Or it can produce a change of state, such as melting or boiling: the energy is used to change the arrangement of the particles and separate them against the forces between them, so their potential energy increases while the temperature stays the same.

Cooling a system does the reverse. Energy is transferred away from the particles, so the internal energy decreases. The temperature falls as the particles slow down, or the substance changes state (condenses or freezes) as the particles move closer together and their potential energy decreases.

Internal energy is about the energy of the particles inside an object, not the energy of the object as a whole. Lifting a book onto a shelf increases its gravitational potential energy store, and throwing a ball increases its kinetic energy store, but neither changes the internal energy of the book or the ball, because the motion and arrangement of the particles inside them are not changed.
keyFacts: Internal energy = total kinetic energy + total potential energy of all the particles.
Internal energy is measured in joules (J).
The kinetic energy of the particles comes from their movement (vibrating or moving around).
The potential energy of the particles comes from the forces between them and their arrangement.
Heating increases the energy of the particles, so internal energy increases.
Heating either raises the temperature or produces a change of state.
When the temperature rises, the kinetic energy of the particles increases.
During a change of state, the potential energy of the particles changes but the temperature stays constant.
Cooling decreases the internal energy of a system.
More particles (more mass) means more internal energy at the same temperature.

keyTerms.definition: The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles that make up a system.
An object or group of objects being studied, such as a beaker of water.
Energy the particles have because they are moving or vibrating.
Energy the particles have because of the forces between them and their positions relative to each other.
Transferring energy to a system because of a temperature difference, which increases the energy of its particles.
A measure of how hot a system is, related to the average kinetic energy of its particles.

workedExamples.title: Adding up internal energy
workedExamples.question: In a small sample of a substance, the particles have a total kinetic energy of 5200 J and a total potential energy of 1800 J. Calculate the internal energy of the sample.
steps: Internal energy = total kinetic energy + total potential energy.

workedExamples.title: Heating during melting
workedExamples.question: The sample is now heated at its melting point and 600 J is transferred to it while it melts. The temperature does not change. State the new internal energy and say which type of particle energy has increased.
steps: Heating increases internal energy by the energy transferred: 7000 + 600 = 7600 J.
The temperature is constant, so the kinetic energy of the particles has not changed (still 5200 J).
So the potential energy has increased by 600 J, to 2400 J.
workedExamples.answer: 7600 J; the potential energy of the particles increased.

workedExamples.title: Comparing internal energy
workedExamples.question: Explain why a swimming pool at 25 °C has more internal energy than a cup of coffee at 80 °C.
steps: Internal energy is the total energy of all the particles.
The coffee particles have more kinetic energy on average, because it is hotter.
But the pool contains far more particles (much greater mass), so the total energy of all its particles is much larger.
workedExamples.answer: The pool has vastly more particles, so its total internal energy is greater even though its temperature is lower.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think internal energy and temperature are the same thing.
misconceptions.right: In fact temperature is related to the average kinetic energy of the particles, while internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles, so it also depends on mass and state.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think heating always makes the temperature rise.
misconceptions.right: In fact during a change of state the energy supplied increases the potential energy of the particles and the temperature stays constant.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a moving or raised object has more internal energy.
misconceptions.right: In fact the kinetic or gravitational potential energy of the whole object is a separate store. Internal energy only counts the energy of the particles inside it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the hottest object always has the most internal energy.
misconceptions.right: In fact a cold object with many more particles (such as an iceberg) can have more internal energy than a small, hot object.

realWorld: Storage heaters use electricity at night to increase the internal energy of dense ceramic blocks, which then heat the room during the day.
Ice in a cool box keeps food cold: energy from the food goes into increasing the potential energy of the ice particles as the ice melts, without the ice warming above 0 °C.
A kettle increases the internal energy of water: first the temperature rises, then at 100 °C the water boils.
examTips: Define internal energy with both parts: 'the total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles in the system'.
Link temperature to kinetic energy and changes of state to potential energy.
When explaining why temperature is constant during melting or boiling, say the energy is increasing the potential energy of the particles, not their kinetic energy.
Use the word 'particles' (or atoms and molecules) in explanations; markers look for it.
summary: Internal energy is the energy stored by the particles in a system.
It is the total kinetic energy plus potential energy of all the particles.
Heating either raises the temperature (kinetic energy increases) or changes the state (potential energy increases).
Internal energy depends on mass, temperature and state.

questions.question: What is the internal energy of a system?
options: The total kinetic energy of all the particles only
The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles
The energy transferred to the surroundings
markScheme: 1 mark: The total kinetic energy and potential energy of all the particles
questions.explanation: Internal energy includes both kinetic energy (movement of particles) and potential energy (forces between particles). Temperature is a separate quantity.

questions.question: What is the unit of internal energy?
markScheme: 1 mark: Joule (J)
questions.explanation: Internal energy is an amount of energy, so it is measured in joules. °C and K measure temperature; watts measure power.

questions.question: What does heating a system do to the energy of its particles?
options: Only changes the mass of the particles
markScheme: 1 mark: Increases it
questions.explanation: Heating transfers energy to the particles, increasing the internal energy of the system.

questions.question: A beaker of water is heated and its temperature rises from 20 °C to 50 °C. Which energy of the particles has increased?
markScheme: 1 mark: Kinetic energy
questions.explanation: A rise in temperature means the particles are moving faster, so their kinetic energy has increased.

questions.question: Heating a substance can either raise its temperature or:
options: change it into a different substance
markScheme: 1 mark: change its state
questions.explanation: The specification states that heating either raises the temperature or produces a change of state. Mass is conserved and internal energy increases, not decreases.

questions.question: Water at 100 °C is boiling and turning into steam at 100 °C. What happens to the internal energy of the water?
options: It stays the same because the temperature is constant
markScheme: 1 mark: It increases
questions.explanation: Energy is being transferred to the water, so its internal energy increases. The energy goes into the potential energy of the particles as they separate, so the temperature does not change.

questions.question: The potential energy of the particles in a substance is due to:
options: the height of the substance above the ground
the forces between the particles and their positions
markScheme: 1 mark: the forces between the particles and their positions
questions.explanation: Particle potential energy depends on the forces between particles and how they are arranged. The height of the whole object affects its gravitational store, not its internal energy.

questions.question: 1 kg of water at 80 °C and 1 kg of water at 20 °C are compared. Which statement is correct?
options: They have the same internal energy because they have the same mass
The water at 20 °C has more internal energy because its particles are closer
The water at 80 °C has less internal energy because its particles are spread out
The water at 80 °C has more internal energy because its particles have more kinetic energy
markScheme: 1 mark: The water at 80 °C has more internal energy because its particles have more kinetic energy
questions.explanation: Same mass and same state, so the only difference is temperature. The hotter water's particles move faster, so it has more internal energy.

questions.question: A cup of hot chocolate cools down on a table. What happens to its internal energy?
markScheme: 1 mark: It decreases
questions.explanation: Energy is transferred to the surroundings, so the particles lose energy and the internal energy decreases.

questions.question: Ice is melting at 0 °C. Which row describes the particles of the ice?
options: Average kinetic energy increases; potential energy stays the same
Average kinetic energy stays the same; potential energy increases
markScheme: 1 mark: Average kinetic energy stays the same; potential energy increases
questions.explanation: The temperature is constant, so the average kinetic energy is unchanged. The energy supplied breaks the regular arrangement and increases the potential energy of the particles.

questions.question: A bath of water at 40 °C and a mug of tea at 80 °C are compared. Which statement is correct?
options: The tea has more internal energy because it is hotter
They must have the same internal energy
The bath has more internal energy because it contains many more particles
The bath has less internal energy because its particles move more slowly
markScheme: 1 mark: The bath has more internal energy because it contains many more particles
questions.explanation: Internal energy is the total for all the particles. The bath has far more particles, so even though each has less kinetic energy on average, the total is much larger.

questions.question: Which of these increases the internal energy of a metal block?
options: Lifting it onto a high shelf
Throwing it so that it moves faster
Moving it to a different room at the same temperature
Hitting it repeatedly with a hammer so it warms up
markScheme: 1 mark: Hitting it repeatedly with a hammer so it warms up
questions.explanation: Hammering does work on the particles and warms the block, increasing the kinetic energy of its particles. Lifting or throwing changes the gravitational or kinetic store of the whole block, not the energy of its particles.

questions.question: Define the internal energy of a system.
markScheme: 1 mark: the total kinetic energy and potential energy
1 mark: of all the particles (atoms and molecules) in the system
questions.explanation: Both types of energy and the word 'particles' are needed for full marks.

questions.question: State the unit used to measure internal energy.
markScheme: 1 mark: joule (J)
questions.explanation: Internal energy is an energy, so it is measured in joules.

questions.question: State the two possible effects of heating a substance.
markScheme: 1 mark: the temperature increases
1 mark: the substance changes state (for example melts or boils)
questions.explanation: Heating increases internal energy, which shows up either as a temperature rise or a change of state.

questions.question: Name the two types of energy that the particles of a system have.
markScheme: 1 mark: kinetic energy
1 mark: potential energy
questions.explanation: Internal energy is the total of these two for all the particles.

questions.question: Explain why the temperature of a block of copper increases when it is heated.
markScheme: 1 mark: energy is transferred to the particles / internal energy increases
1 mark: the particles vibrate faster so their kinetic energy increases, and temperature depends on the (average) kinetic energy of the particles
questions.explanation: A rise in temperature is a rise in the average kinetic energy of the particles.

questions.question: Ice at 0 °C is heated but its temperature does not rise until all of it has melted. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the energy is used to change the state / change the arrangement of particles (overcome forces between them)
1 mark: so the potential energy of the particles increases, not their kinetic energy, so temperature stays constant
questions.explanation: During a change of state, the extra internal energy goes into the potential energy of the particles.

questions.question: Water in a freezer cools and then freezes. Describe what happens to the internal energy of the water and explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the internal energy decreases
1 mark: energy is transferred from the water to the surroundings, so the particles slow down (kinetic energy falls) and then their potential energy falls as they freeze into a fixed arrangement
questions.explanation: Cooling is the reverse of heating: kinetic energy falls as temperature drops, then potential energy falls during freezing.

questions.question: A hot metal block is placed in a beaker of cold water. Describe the change in internal energy of the block and of the water.
acceptedAnswers: energy transferred from block to water
markScheme: 1 mark: the internal energy of the block decreases
1 mark: the internal energy of the water increases (energy is transferred from the block to the water)
questions.explanation: Energy is transferred by heating from the hotter block to the cooler water until they reach the same temperature.

questions.question: A footballer kicks a ball so that it moves at 20 m/s. Explain why this does not increase the internal energy of the ball.
acceptedAnswers: internal energy is energy of particles
markScheme: 1 mark: the energy goes into the kinetic energy store of the ball as a whole
1 mark: internal energy is the energy of the particles inside the ball, and their (random) motion and arrangement are not changed by the ball moving
questions.explanation: Internal energy only counts the energy of the particles relative to each other, not the movement of the whole object.

questions.question: Suggest why a large iceberg at −5 °C can have more internal energy than a kettle of boiling water.
markScheme: 1 mark: the iceberg has a far greater mass / many more particles
1 mark: internal energy is the total energy of all the particles, so the large number of particles outweighs the lower energy per particle
questions.explanation: Internal energy is a total, not an average. Temperature is the average, which is why the kettle is hotter.

questions.question: Steam at 100 °C condenses into water at 100 °C. Explain what happens to the kinetic energy and the potential energy of the particles.
markScheme: 1 mark: the kinetic energy (average) stays the same because the temperature does not change
1 mark: the potential energy decreases as the particles move closer together into the liquid arrangement (so internal energy decreases)
questions.explanation: Condensing releases energy to the surroundings; the drop in internal energy is all in the potential energy of the particles.

questions.question:
A block of ice at −20 °C is heated steadily until it becomes water at 30 °C.
Explain what is meant by internal energy and describe how the internal energy of the ice and water changes during this process. Refer to the kinetic energy and potential energy of the particles.
markScheme: Indicative content: internal energy is the total kinetic and potential energy of all the particles; heating transfers energy to the particles so internal energy increases throughout; from −20 °C to 0 °C the temperature of the ice rises, particles vibrate faster, kinetic energy increases; at 0 °C the ice melts; temperature stays constant; energy increases the potential energy of the particles as the regular arrangement breaks down; kinetic energy unchanged during melting; from 0 °C to 30 °C the temperature of the water rises; particles move faster, kinetic energy increases; mass stays the same throughout.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a correct definition and a full, logically ordered description of all three stages, linking temperature rises to kinetic energy and the change of state to potential energy.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a definition and a description of at least two stages, with some correct links to kinetic or potential energy.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'the ice gets hotter and melts' or 'internal energy increases'.
No relevant content: 0 marks.
questions.explanation: Break the process into stages: warming ice, melting, warming water. Each temperature rise is kinetic energy; the change of state is potential energy.

questions.question: Compare 1 kg of liquid water at 100 °C with 1 kg of steam at 100 °C in terms of the motion, arrangement and energy of their particles, and state which has more internal energy.
markScheme: Indicative content: same temperature so the average kinetic energy of the particles is the same; same mass so the same number of particles; in water the particles are close together and move around each other; in steam the particles are far apart and move randomly and quickly; energy had to be supplied to turn water into steam to separate the particles; steam particles have more potential energy; so steam has more internal energy.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct comparison of kinetic energy (same) and potential energy (greater in steam), with particle arrangement, and the correct conclusion that steam has more internal energy.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct comparison of arrangement, or a conclusion with limited explanation.
No relevant content: 0 marks.
questions.explanation: The trap is to say they have the same internal energy because they are at the same temperature. The steam has the extra potential energy that was supplied when the water boiled.

questions.question: A pan of cold water is placed on an electric hob and left until it boils. Describe how the internal energy of the water changes and what happens to its particles, from when it is cold until it is boiling.
markScheme: Indicative content: energy is transferred from the hob to the water by heating; internal energy of the water increases; at first the temperature rises because the particles move faster, so their kinetic energy increases; when the water reaches 100 °C it boils; the temperature stays constant while boiling; energy now increases the potential energy of particles as they separate to form steam; the internal energy keeps increasing.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a clear description of both stages (temperature rise and boiling) linked to kinetic and potential energy of particles.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states that internal energy increases or that the water gets hotter and boils, with little reference to particles.
No relevant content: 0 marks.
questions.explanation: Two stages, two kinds of particle energy. Internal energy rises throughout.
